summary.text: Oceanic trenches are long, narrow depressions in the ocean floor, typically 50 to 100 km wide and 3 to 4 km below the seafloor around them.
They mark convergent plate boundaries, where a bent slab of one plate begins to sink beneath another plate.
Fluid from sediments on the sinking slab comes back up at trenches, forming mud volcanoes and cold seeps that support communities of chemotrophic microbes.

facts.label: Deepest measured point
facts.value: Challenger Deep, 10,994 m below sea level

facts.label: Distance from volcanic arc
facts.value: About 200 km, running parallel to it

items.prompt: A survey maps a long seafloor depression with steep sides and a wide, flat bottom. Judging by shape alone, what is it?
items.explain: Troughs have steep sides and flat bottoms, while trenches have a V-shaped profile.

items.prompt: A plate carrying a continent drifts into a trench and its buoyant continental crust reaches the edge. What happens next?

options.label: The continent sinks into the mantle
Subduction halts and the plates collide
The plates reverse and pull apart

items.explain: When buoyant continental crust enters a trench, subduction stops and the area becomes a continental collision zone, like the Himalayas.

items.prompt: Off the northwest coast of North America, the Cascadia subduction zone shows no depression on the seafloor at all. How do geologists classify it?

options.label: Still a trench, buried under sediment
A trough, because it has no depth
A pull-apart basin on a transform fault
A former trench that has stopped working

items.explain: Cascadia is completely filled with sediment, but its underlying plate-tectonic structure is still an oceanic trench.

items.prompt: A ship leaves a chain of volcanic islands and heads out toward the open ocean, at right angles to the chain. Roughly how far will it go before crossing the trench?
items.explain: Trenches lie on the oceanward side of island arcs, generally parallel to the volcanic arc and about 200 km from it.

items.prompt: If you traced every oceanic trench on a world map, which ocean would most of them surround?
items.explain: Most of the roughly 50,000 km of trenches lie around the Pacific Ocean, with others in the eastern Indian Ocean and a few other places.

items.prompt: Far from sunlight, mud volcanoes and cold seeps along trenches support whole communities of life. What are these communities based on?
items.explain: Fluid returning to the surface at trenches feeds mud volcanoes and cold seeps, which support biomes based on chemotrophic microorganisms.

pack.title: Where the Seafloor Goes Under
pack.question: What makes an oceanic trench, and how do you tell one apart?

beats.title: Where the Seafloor Goes Under
beats.hook: The deepest spots on Earth are long, narrow slots in the seafloor, and some trenches are buried so completely you cannot see them at all.

beats.prompt: A plate is sinking into a trench, pulling a continent toward it. The buoyant continental crust reaches the trench. What happens?
beats.explain: When buoyant continental crust enters a trench, subduction halts and the area becomes a zone of continental collision, as in the Himalayas.

choices.label: Subduction stops and a collision zone forms
A new volcanic arc opens behind the continent
choices.feedback: Arcs go with active subduction, which is what stops here.

choices.label: The trench simply gets deeper
choices.feedback: Nothing more sinks there; subduction comes to a halt instead.

choices.label: The continent is dragged down into the mantle
choices.feedback: Oceanic lithosphere is recycled this way, but buoyant continental crust is not.

beats.prompt: Some 'troughs' are really trenches, and some are not. Sort each one.
beats.explain: Makran is a partly filled trench and Cascadia a fully buried one, while the other troughs are a forearc basin, an extensional basin and a pull-apart basin.

beats.prompt: Match each seafloor feature to what it is.

right.label: Forearc basin of a subduction zone
Pull-apart basin in a transform fault zone
Steep sides and a flat bottom

beats.explain: Shape separates trenches from troughs, and the troughs that look like trenches turn out to be other tectonic structures.

paragraphs.heading: What a trench is
paragraphs.text: Ocean trenches are long, narrow dips in the ocean floor that stand out clearly. Most are 50 to 100 km wide and sit 3 to 4 km below the seafloor around them, yet they can run for thousands of kilometres. Worldwide there are about 50,000 km of them, mostly around the Pacific, with some in the eastern Indian Ocean and a few elsewhere. More than 50 major trenches together cover about 1.9 million km², roughly 0.5% of the oceans. The greatest ocean depth ever measured, 10,994 m below sea level, is in the Challenger Deep of the Mariana Trench.

paragraphs.heading: Where plates meet
paragraphs.text: Trenches are a feature of plate tectonics. They mark places where two plates move toward each other, at anywhere from a few millimetres to more than ten centimetres a year. A trench is where a bent slab of one plate starts to sink beneath the other, a process called subduction. At least one of the plates is oceanic, and it dives under the other to be recycled in Earth's mantle. Trenches usually run parallel to a line of volcanoes, called a volcanic arc, about 200 km away.

paragraphs.heading: Trench or trough
paragraphs.text: Trenches have a V-shaped cross-section, unlike troughs, which are long seafloor dips with steep sides and flat bottoms. The line can blur: trenches partly filled in, such as the Makran Trough, are sometimes called troughs. Some trenches are buried completely, like the Cascadia subduction zone, which is full of sediment and shows no dip at all, yet in plate terms it is still a trench. Other troughs only look like trenches; the Cayman Trough, for example, is a pull-apart basin inside a transform fault zone.

paragraphs.heading: Seeps and life
paragraphs.text: Much of the fluid trapped in sediments on the sinking slab comes back up at the trench. There it builds mud volcanoes and cold seeps, which host unusual communities based on chemotrophic microorganisms. There is worry that plastic debris is collecting in trenches and putting these communities at risk.

paragraphs.heading: When continents collide
paragraphs.text: Trenches are related to continental collision zones such as the Himalayas, but they are not the same. In a collision zone, continental crust goes into the subduction zone. When buoyant continental crust reaches a trench, subduction stops and the area turns into a zone of continental collision.

paragraphs.heading: Mapping the deep
paragraphs.text: Only in the late 1940s and 1950s were trenches clearly defined. Little was known of ocean depths before the Challenger expedition of 1872–1876, which made 492 deep soundings and, at station 225, found the Challenger Deep, which we now know sits at the Mariana Trench's southern end. Laying telegraph cables across the seafloor in the late 1800s and early 1900s gave another reason to measure depths better. Johnstone first used "trench" in its modern sense in his 1923 textbook An Introduction to Oceanography. World War II in the Pacific then brought great improvements in depth maps, especially in the western Pacific.
